extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and anyone studying logic or critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, classifying, and diagnosing errors in reasoning (inductive and deductive) using a five-part taxonomy of fallacies and related diagnostics for spotting tacit premises, ambiguity, and misuse of a priori intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fivefold classification of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: A top-level taxonomy dividing erroneous reasoning into five classes: (1) Fallacies of Simple Inspection (à priori), (2) Fallacies of Observation (inductive fallacies from erroneous facts), (3) Fallacies of Generalization (inductive fallacies where true facts are inconclusive), (4) Fallacies of Ratiocination (deductive fallacies where premises do not support conclusion), and (5) Fallacies of Confusion (errors arising from indistinct or shifting conception of premises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this schema to diagnose the kind of error in an argument by asking whether the supposed evidence is immediate inspection, particular facts, or general propositions, and whether the evidence is false or true-but-inconclusive. The scheme helps place a given erroneous argument into the most probable class, while recognizing overlap among classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (à priori fallacies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions embraced as self-evident or accepted without proof (or with only intrinsic verisimilitude), i.e., conclusions taken as requiring no external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for tacit acceptance of claims as 'self-evident' or derived from intuition alone. Manifestations include mistaking ideas for realities (treating properties of our conceptions as properties of things), personifying abstractions (treating names as distinct entities), inferring truth from conceivability, or assuming that what we find easiest to conceive is likeliest true. Examples discussed: popular superstitions, Cartesian and Leibnitzian metaphysical moves, and historical scientific errors. Practical caution: do not accept intuitions as proof; seek empirical or argumentative support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies where the facts on which induction proceeds are erroneous (mal-observation, non-observation, or false inference from intermediate marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as failures in ascertainment of facts. When evaluating inductive claims, check whether observations were accurately made or whether inferences from marks are warranted. Errors can be direct (bad observation) or indirect (erroneous inference about observed marks). Remedy: improve empirical ascertainment and inspect intermediate signs for their probative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies in which the observed facts are correct but the generalization drawn from them is not warranted (overgeneralization or inferring a unique cause from an effect without considering alternatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check sample size, representativeness, alternative explanations, and whether the jump from particular to general is justified. Example: concluding government tyranny from general national distress without proper justification. Remedy: require stronger inductive support before forming broad generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of deduction in which premises (though sometimes true) do not bear out the attempted conclusion—vicious argumentation counter to syllogistic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the logical form and distribution of terms; check for undistributed middle terms and invalid syllogistic moves. Supply every suppressed premise and test whether, when fully stated, the syllogism is valid. If not, the argument is a ratiocination fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors whose chief characteristic is indistinct conception or vagueness—arising from failure to state the question properly, ambiguity of terms, or unconsciously substituting different premises during argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify terms and premises; restate the argument in unambiguous language. Many real-world fallacies, when fully and clearly set out, reduce to some other class, but where confusion is the dominant feature treat it as this class. Watch for equivocation, shifting meanings, and reasoning in a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressed premises and tacit assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments often omit intermediate links; one premise is usually suppressed, and the error may lie in that tacit assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect fallacy, explicitly supply the silent premise(s). The confuter should ask (Socratic interrogation) what unstated assumption is needed to make the conclusion follow. Whately's example: from 'the country is distressed' to 'the government is tyrannical' requires a suppressed premise which may be false or irrelevant. When multiple suppressed premises could be supplied, observers may interpret the argument differently—resolve by forcing explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent evidence: particular facts vs foregone generalizations; false vs inconclusive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent evidence in an argument may be (a) particular facts (induction) or (b) previously assumed generalizations (deduction). In either case, evidence may be false or true but fail to support the conclusion (inconclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, first classify the apparent evidence type and then ask whether it is factually correct and whether, if correct, it is sufficient to warrant the conclusion. This two-step diagnosis distinguishes Observation (wrong facts) from Generalization (insufficient support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies tend to cluster; ambiguous assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual erroneous arguments frequently exhibit features of more than one class of fallacy; strict classification can be arbitrary, and most fallacies might ultimately be referred to confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-insist on exclusive labeling; determine the most probable seat of error given the nature of the argument and the tendencies of human thought in the circumstances. Use pragmatic judgment to decide which class best explains the error and guide correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification / personification of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating names of qualities or general terms as if they denote distinct, objective entities (e.g., treating 'whiteness' or 'man in general' as a separate substance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that having a name implies a corresponding external thing. Recognize the difference between linguistic/conceptual convenience and ontological commitment. This error produces mysticism and confuses general language with evidence of distinct entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equating conceivability with truth (and inconceivability with falsity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that because something can be conceived clearly it must exist, or because something is inconceivable it cannot be true (e.g., 'whatever is inconceivable must be false').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the move from conceivability to real-world existence or vice versa. Historical examples: antipodes and Copernican objections, Newton's struggle with action at a distance. Conceptual limitations of the thinker are not limits of nature; do not treat them as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to simplicity as proof ('nature acts by the simplest means')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the hypothesis which is easiest to conceive or the simplest in form is likeliest to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: empirical history shows simple, intuitively pleasing hypotheses (e.g., heavenly circles) can be wrong and require ad hoc complications. Use simplicity as one heuristic among many, not as decisive proof; demand empirical corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming mental incapacity equals impossibility in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting hypotheses on the grounds that they seem 'absurd' or 'inconceivable' to present faculties, thereby excluding possible truths (e.g., asserting matter cannot think because we cannot conceive it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not bar proposals solely on the basis of current imaginative or conceptual difficulty. Recognize that expansions of experience and imaginative power in future investigators may render formerly inconceivable combinations conceivable.
